cards.front: Physiological anaemia of pregnancy stays [___] on the film, so a falling mean cell volume instead points to superimposed iron deficiency.
cards.context:
Pure dilution is normocytic. Falling mean cell volume suggests an additional cause, commonly iron deficiency, but can also reflect thalassaemia.

Interpret ferritin with cell-size trends, symptoms and inflammation. Low ferritin supports iron deficiency; neither a falling nor normal cell volume alone establishes iron status.

cards.front: Normal pregnancy arterial blood gas (ABG) shows a chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis with PaCO₂ around 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ around [___] mmol/L.
cards.context: The driver is progesterone, which acts on the central respiratory chemoreceptors to raise tidal volume by ~40% (rate is unchanged). The kidneys then excrete bicarbonate to keep pH near the upper limit of normal.

cards.front: Visible jaundice before [___] hours of age warrants prompt investigation rather than a diagnosis of physiological jaundice.
cards.context: Jaundice starting before 24 hours is a red flag for a pathological cause and needs prompt assessment. Physiological jaundice usually starts later.

cards.front: The ideal fetal presentation is flexed vertex, occiput anterior; the smallest presenting diameter is the [___] (~9.5 cm).
cards.context:
Full flexion presents the suboccipitobregmatic diameter, about 9.5 cm. Occiput anterior describes the direction of the occiput; flexion describes the head's attitude.

Deflexed vertex presents a larger diameter; persistent brow is particularly obstructive. Fully extended face presents the submentobregmatic diameter, also about 9.5 cm.

Occiput posterior often accompanies deflexion and can prolong labour. Face presentation is not automatically too wide: chin position and labour progress determine whether vaginal birth is possible.

cards.front: Vitamin K prophylaxis for a newborn of at least 1500 g: preferred [___] dose 1 mg at birth; if declined, oral regimen is three doses over 4 weeks.
cards.context:
VKDB (formerly HDN) affects neonates because the liver doesn't synthesise factors II, VII, IX, X without vitamin K, and breast milk has minimal vitamin K.

For a newborn of at least 1500 g, IM vitamin K 1 mg at birth is a single, near-100% effective dose with no compliance issues. QCG uses 0.5 mg IM below 1500 g.

cards.front: The WNHS scalp lactate band of 4.2–4.8 mmol/L is classified as [___].
cards.context: Both endpoints are included in the published table. Interpret the trend and clinical situation, not the number alone.

cards.front: For a stable woman with hyperemesis and prolonged poor intake, the treating team gives IV thiamine before a planned [___] infusion to reduce Wernicke encephalopathy risk.
cards.context:
Prolonged poor intake in hyperemesis can deplete thiamine. NSW guidance advises supplementation before planned glucose-containing fluids and checking sodium first.

This is not a rule to delay emergency treatment of hypoglycaemia. Arrange prompt thiamine alongside urgent care; deficiency can cause serious neurological harm, but harm is not inevitable.

Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes in glucose oxidation, so repletion before a glucose load reduces Wernicke risk.

cards.front: A dating scan, when done, is recommended at [___] weeks; it confirms viability, dates the pregnancy, and detects multiple gestation.
cards.context:
Australian guidance recommends a dating scan, when done, between 8+0 and 13+6 weeks. It confirms viability, dates pregnancy by CRL, and identifies multiple pregnancy/chorionicity.

Book it in this narrow window because CRL dating is more accurate than later biparietal diameter/head circumference estimates, and chorionicity is easiest to assess while membranes are clearly visible.

cards.front: Gestational diabetes is screened with a 75 g OGTT at [___] weeks.
cards.context:
Glucose intolerance first recognised in pregnancy, screened around 24–28 weeks with an oral glucose tolerance test.

It drives macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and shoulder dystocia, and flags future maternal type 2 risk.

cards.front: Shoulder dystocia mnemonic HELPERR — Help, Evaluate episiotomy, [___], Pressure (suprapubic, NEVER fundal), Enter, Remove posterior arm, Roll.
cards.context:
Call the obstetric team immediately. McRoberts means flexing the hips so the thighs approach the abdomen; suprapubic pressure helps free the impacted shoulder.

Never use fundal pressure: it can worsen impaction. The mnemonic supports trained teamwork, not rigid delays between manoeuvres. Students should assist only under direction.

[NSW shoulder dystocia guidance](https://www.seslhd.health.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/shoulder2020.pdf).

cards.front: In a pregnancy of unknown location, a plateau or fall in βhCG over 48 hours means the pregnancy is [___], whether it is intrauterine or ectopic.
cards.context:
In pregnancy of unknown location, compare serum βhCG about 48 hours apart and repeat transvaginal ultrasound; the trend does not locate the pregnancy by itself.

A rise greater than 63% suggests a developing IUP, while a smaller rise, plateau or fall needs prompt clinical review. A viable pregnancy does not have to double in 48 hours.

No visible IUP above a locally used discriminatory level raises concern for ectopic pregnancy but does not prove it without the full clinical and imaging picture.

cards.front: The cardinal movements of labour in order are engagement, descent, [___], internal rotation, extension, restitution, and external rotation.
cards.context:
The cardinal movements describe how the fetal head and body navigate the pelvis during vaginal delivery.

In order: engagement → descent → flexion → internal rotation → extension → restitution → external rotation → expulsion.

The head presents a smaller diameter by flexing, rotates internally to fit the AP pelvic diameter, then extends under the symphysis pubis to deliver.

cards.front: Newborn vitamin K is a single 1 mg IM dose; it prevents late deficiency bleeding at 2-12 weeks, half of which is [___].
cards.context:
Newborns are vitamin-K deficient (poor placental transfer, sterile gut, minimal K in breast milk), and factors II/VII/IX/X need K-dependent gamma-carboxylation — so deficiency causes haemorrhagic disease (VKDB).

Two forms: classical (days 2-7) and the more dangerous late-onset (2-12 weeks, 50% intracranial haemorrhage); standard prophylaxis 1 mg IM at birth, near-100% effective for both.

Oral regimens (3 doses over 4 weeks) are an alternative if parents decline IM, but need adherence and are less reliable for late VKDB. The 1992 IM-vit-K/leukaemia link has been refuted — document any refusal.

cards.front: [___] uterus is blood infiltration of the myometrium from severe placental abruption, which can contribute to uterine atony and PPH; risk of DIC from disrupted decidua.
cards.context:
Couvelaire uterus (uteroplacental apoplexy) is the visual signature of severe placental abruption at caesarean — blood has dissected from retroplacental haematoma into myometrium, producing a purple, bruised uterus.

Severe abruption also releases tissue factor + procoagulants from disrupted decidua → DIC (consumptive coagulopathy: falling platelets, falling fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, prolonged INR/APTT).

Couvelaire appearance alone does not require hysterectomy; treat ongoing haemorrhage and coagulopathy. [Clinical report](https://doi.org/10.1177/87564793231224787).

cards.front: Three weeks after birth, a mother remains tearful, has lost enjoyment and struggles with daily tasks. Her GP should assess for [___].
cards.context:
Baby blues usually settle within two weeks. Persistent symptoms with loss of pleasure or impaired function need clinical assessment; a screening score alone does not establish the diagnosis.

Assess safety and support promptly. Suicidal thoughts, psychosis or concern about infant safety require urgent escalation.

cards.front: Twenty minutes after a vaginal birth, a woman has lost 800 mL. The placenta is complete, the perineum and vagina are intact, and the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus. The most likely cause is [___].
cards.context:
The four Ts of primary PPH are tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin. Poor tone (atony) causes most, about 70%.

A complete placenta and an intact genital tract point away from tissue and trauma. Rub up the fundus and give uterotonics.

cards.front: At the first-trimester scan, a T sign in a twin pregnancy indicates [___].
cards.context: The T sign is a membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle without an intervening tissue wedge, indicating monochorionic diamniotic twins.

cards.front: Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia: loading 4 g IV over 20 min, then [___] infusion until 24 hours after birth or the last seizure. Earliest toxicity sign is loss of patellar reflexes.
cards.context:
Magnesium is anticonvulsant via NMDA blockade and cerebral vasodilation.

In women already fitting, it prevented recurrence better than phenytoin or diazepam (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial); in pre-eclampsia, Magpie halved eclampsia against placebo.

Reflexes go first. Stop the infusion if they are lost or breathing stays at 12/min or less for 15 min, check the level (toxic above 3.5 mmol/L) and give calcium gluconate.

cards.front: Australian newborn bloodspot screening has detected [___] since the 1980s–90s, using a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen followed by CFTR gene testing.
cards.context:
Early diagnosis allows enzyme replacement, salt supplements and lung surveillance before symptoms.

A positive screen is confirmed with a sweat test.

cards.front: A single serum β-hCG can confirm pregnancy, but it cannot by itself establish [___] or an intrauterine site.
cards.context:
A level greater than 5 IU/L means a pregnancy is present. It does not say the pregnancy is viable.

The same single result cannot exclude an intrauterine pregnancy. Location needs ultrasound, with a repeat level in 48 hours if she is stable.

That is why a number above the threshold is only the first step in early pregnancy assessment.

cards.front: Crowning is recognised when the extending fetal head distends the perineum and no longer [___] between contractions.
cards.context:
Crowning is the finding that the extending head has stretched the perineum and no longer slips back when the contraction ends.

Extension is how the head reaches the outlet. The name crowning applies once the head stays visible between contractions.

cards.front: Delayed meconium passage with distal obstruction from congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells suggests [___].
cards.context:
No meconium by 24–48 hours in a term baby warrants assessment for distal obstruction. Distension or bilious vomiting increases concern; do not wait for the time limit if these develop.

Consider Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus associated with cystic fibrosis, meconium plug and anorectal malformation. Inspect the anus; delayed meconium alone does not identify the cause.

cards.front: A woman before pregnancy is at the BMI threshold for obesity, which is [___] kg/m².
cards.context: The BMI threshold defining obesity before pregnancy is 30 kg/m². Higher BMI is associated with gestational diabetes, hypertensive disease, thrombosis and stillbirth.

cards.front: For adult late latent syphilis without neurological involvement, the benzathine penicillin course consists of [___].
cards.context:
Treponemal tests usually remain positive after treatment. RPR trends help assess response; a fourfold fall supports an adequate response but does not replace clinical review or assessment for reinfection.

Late latent or unknown-duration infection needs three weekly intramuscular doses. Neurological, eye or ear involvement needs urgent specialist assessment and a different regimen.

Syphilis in pregnancy needs urgent specialist care and penicillin according to stage. Repeat serology checks response and reinfection; do not treat a single result as proof of cure.

cards.front: Erb's palsy is a C5-C6 brachial plexus injury producing 'waiter's tip' — arm adducted, [___] rotated, elbow extended, wrist flexed.
cards.context:
Erb's palsy = upper trunk (C5-C6) brachial plexus injury, classically from excessive lateral head traction during difficult delivery (often after shoulder dystocia).

Deficit map: C5-C6 supplies deltoid, biceps, brachialis, supinator, supraspinatus, infraspinatus — arm hangs adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed ('waiter's tip').

Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1) is the lower-trunk injury → 'claw hand' with absent grasp.

cards.front: Cord prolapse: position the patient in [___] or knee-chest and elevate the presenting part; if vaginal birth is not imminent and the fetal heart rate is abnormal, arrange a category 1 caesarean.
cards.context:
Cord prolapse can rapidly compromise fetal oxygenation. Immediately use steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest and manually elevate the presenting part.

If vaginal birth is not imminent and the trace is suspicious or pathological, expedite category 1 caesarean: immediate threat to life; aim for birth within 30 minutes of the decision. A normal trace may allow category 2.

For prolonged transfer, bladder filling with 500-750 mL saline can maintain elevation. Minimise cord handling to avoid vasospasm.

cards.front: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) is a [___] test analysing cell-free fetal DNA from 10 weeks; positive results require invasive CVS/amniocentesis confirmation.
cards.context:
NIPT analyses cell-free fetal DNA fragments shed by placental trophoblast into maternal blood. The 10-week floor is when fetal fraction is high enough to call reliably; earlier risks an uninterpretable 'no result'.

It is a SCREENING test, not diagnostic — the DNA is placental, not directly fetal, so a positive can be confined placental mosaicism, a vanishing twin, or maternal mosaicism.

That is why a positive must be confirmed by an invasive karyotype (CVS or amniocentesis) before any irreversible decision.

cards.front: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy [___]. The chromosome involved is the smallest autosome. Risk rises with maternal age.
cards.context:
Maternal age drives aneuploidy risk — oocyte meiotic spindle errors accumulate (non-disjunction during meiosis I dominates).

T21 (Down) is the commonest viable autosomal trisomy. Chromosome 21 is the smallest autosome; size alone does not explain viability. [NIH overview](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/down-syndrome).

cards.front: Magnesium sulfate given before imminent very-preterm birth reduces the baby's risk of [___].
cards.context: A second antenatal role for magnesium (separate from eclampsia seizure prophylaxis): given before imminent very-preterm birth it is fetal neuroprotective, reducing cerebral palsy in survivors.

cards.front: Most complete molar pregnancies are karyotype 46,XX (paternal/androgenetic); partial moles are usually 69,XXY; ~[___]% of complete moles progress to GTN.
cards.context:
A complete mole usually forms when sperm fertilises an empty ovum and its chromosomes duplicate; less often two sperm fertilise it. There is no fetal tissue.

A partial mole usually forms when two sperm fertilise a normal ovum, producing a triploid conception (most often 69,XXY) with abnormal fetal tissue.

GTN follows 15-20% of complete moles in most texts; RANZCOG quotes 15-25%, against 0.5-4% after a partial mole.
